subject: Science
title: Structure of the Atom
summary: This chapter traces how the atom's model developed from Thomson to Rutherford to Bohr, then settles into the working picture you use for the rest of school chemistry: protons and neutrons in a tiny nucleus, electrons in shells around it, and the rules (2n², valency, atomic number, isotopes) that come out of that picture.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 9 has no board exam, so there is no official marks weightage. In school tests and the final exam it is treated as a core chemistry chapter, usually worth 8-11 marks across MCQ, VSA, SA and one LA/case question.

question_types.note: Charge and mass of sub-atomic particles, who discovered what, canal rays, 2n² calculations, isotope/isobar identification.
Pairs a fact about atomic structure with its reason, e.g. why an atom is neutral, why isotopes have identical chemical behaviour.
Define a term, state a postulate, or do a one-line electron/neutron count.
Explain a model (Thomson/Rutherford/Bohr) in brief, or work out valency/electron distribution for a given element.
Full description of the alpha-particle scattering experiment with observations and conclusions, or Bohr's model with a labelled diagram.
A short passage on isotopes/isobars or an experiment, followed by 4 sub-questions.

hot_topics: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment — set-up, three observations, three conclusions
Drawbacks of Rutherford's model and how Bohr fixed them
Bohr-Bury scheme: distributing electrons in shells using 2n²
Finding valency from the number of valence electrons
Atomic number, mass number and writing the ᴬZX symbol
Isotopes vs isobars — definition, examples, and uses of isotopes
Thomson's plum-pudding model and why the atom is electrically neutral
Discovery and properties of electron, proton and neutron

sections.heading: 4.1 Charged Particles in Matter
sections.body:
By the late 1800s, experiments with electricity through gases and salt solutions showed that matter contains charged particles, so the atom cannot be the indivisible, uncuttable thing its name (Greek 'a-tomio', not to be cut) originally meant.

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron from cathode ray tube experiments. Cathode rays travel from the negative electrode to the positive electrode, and in an electric field they bend towards the positive plate, showing they carry a negative charge. Thomson found this negative particle is present in atoms of every element, so it is a universal, fundamental constituent of matter. An electron carries a charge of −1 unit (−1.6 × 10−19 C) and a mass about 1/2000th that of a hydrogen atom.

E. Goldstein discovered canal rays (also called anode rays) — streams of positively charged particles produced in a discharge tube with a perforated cathode, moving opposite to cathode rays. This led to the discovery of the proton, a particle of charge +1 unit (+1.6 × 10−19 C) and mass about 1 atomic mass unit (u), roughly 2000 times the mass of an electron.

Since ordinary matter is electrically neutral, an atom must carry equal numbers of positive and negative charges: the positive charge of its protons exactly balances the negative charge of its electrons.
sections.tip: A one-mark question often just asks 'who discovered the electron/proton and by which rays' — pair Thomson–cathode rays–electron and Goldstein–canal rays–proton and you will not confuse them.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Thomson's Model of an Atom
sections.body:
Thomson proposed that an atom is a uniformly positively charged sphere, with electrons embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon or plums in a pudding — this is why it is called the plum-pudding model (also the watermelon model).

The important features are: (i) the positive charge is spread throughout the sphere, not concentrated anywhere; (ii) the negatively charged electrons are studded inside this sphere; (iii) the magnitude of the positive charge equals the total negative charge of the electrons, so the atom as a whole is electrically neutral.

This model could explain the electrical neutrality of the atom, but it failed to explain the results of later experiments — particularly Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, which showed that positive charge is not spread out but concentrated in a tiny region.
sections.tip: If asked 'how does Thomson's model explain the neutrality of the atom', write the equal-and-opposite-charge line explicitly — that single sentence is the marking point.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Rutherford's Model of an Atom
sections.body:
Ernest Rutherford directed fast-moving alpha (α) particles (doubly charged helium ions, He2+) at a thin gold foil (about 100 nm thick) with a circular fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around it to detect where the particles landed. This is the alpha-particle scattering experiment.

Observations: (i) Most of the fast-moving alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection. (ii) Some particles were deflected by small angles. (iii) A very small fraction (about 1 in 12000) bounced back almost 180°.

Conclusions: (i) Since most alpha particles passed through undeflected, most of the space inside the atom is empty. (ii) Since a few positively charged, fast alpha particles were deflected, they must have been repelled by a small region of concentrated positive charge — this region is the nucleus. (iii) Since a very few particles bounced straight back, nearly all the mass of the atom is concentrated in this very small nucleus.

From these results Rutherford proposed a new model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre carrying almost the entire mass of the atom, with electrons revolving around it in circular orbits, much as planets revolve around the sun. The size of the nucleus is very small compared to the size of the atom (roughly 1/100000th).

Drawback: according to the electromagnetic theory of that time, a charged particle moving in a circular path (an accelerating charge) must continuously radiate energy. If an electron kept losing energy this way, it would spiral inward and eventually fall into the nucleus, making the atom unstable. But atoms are known to be stable, so Rutherford's model could not explain this.
sections.tip: The alpha-scattering LA question is asked almost every year in some form — memorise the three observations and the three conclusions as matched pairs, and draw the gold-foil/screen set-up with the deflected paths.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 Bohr's Model of Atom
sections.body:
To fix the instability problem of Rutherford's model, Niels Bohr proposed a new model with two main postulates. (i) Only certain special orbits, called discrete orbits or shells, are allowed inside the atom; these are the only orbits in which an electron is permitted to move. (ii) While revolving in these fixed, discrete orbits, an electron does not radiate energy, even though it is accelerating.

These shells, or energy levels, are represented by the letters K, L, M, N, ... going outward from the nucleus, corresponding to n = 1, 2, 3, 4, .... An electron stays at a fixed energy in a given shell; it neither loses nor gains energy as long as it stays in that shell, which is why the atom is stable in Bohr's picture. Electrons can jump between shells only by absorbing or releasing a fixed amount of energy.

Bohr's model gave a working, stable picture of the atom that matched the chemistry of the elements very well, and it is the model used through the rest of school-level chemistry (shells, valence electrons, valency), even though the modern quantum-mechanical model has since replaced the idea of a sharp circular orbit with a probability cloud.
sections.tip: For a 5-mark question, state both postulates clearly, name the shells K, L, M, N and draw a nucleus with 2-3 concentric circular orbits with electrons marked as dots on them.

sections.heading: 4.2.4 Neutrons
sections.body:
A third sub-atomic particle, the neutron, was discovered by J. Chadwick in 1932. Neutrons are present in the nucleus of all atoms except the ordinary hydrogen atom (protium), which has only one proton and no neutron.

A neutron has no charge (it is electrically neutral) and its mass is nearly equal to that of a proton, about 1 u. Together, protons and neutrons make up the mass of the atom and are collectively called nucleons. The number of neutrons in an atom is found by subtracting the atomic number (number of protons) from the mass number: number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

formulas.expr: number of neutrons (n) = mass number (A) − atomic number (Z)

sections.tip: A common one-mark trap: 'which sub-atomic particle has no charge' — the answer is neutron, not electron (electron is negatively charged, not neutral).

sections.heading: 4.3 How are Electrons Distributed in Different Orbits (Shells)?
sections.body:
Bohr and Bury worked out the rules for filling electrons into shells, known as the Bohr-Bury scheme. The shells are numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ... from the nucleus outward and named K, L, M, N, .... The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in a shell is given by the formula 2n2.

So the K shell (n = 1) can hold a maximum of 2 electrons, the L shell (n = 2) a maximum of 8, the M shell (n = 3) a maximum of 18, and the N shell (n = 4) a maximum of 32.

Two more practical rules apply at the school level: (i) the outermost shell of an atom can hold a maximum of 8 electrons (even if 2n2 allows more); (ii) electrons are not accommodated in a given shell unless the inner shells are filled first, i.e. shells are filled in a stepwise manner starting from K.

For example, sodium (atomic number 11) has the electron distribution 2, 8, 1 — 2 in K, 8 in L, and the remaining 1 in M. Magnesium (atomic number 12) is 2, 8, 2. Argon (atomic number 18) is 2, 8, 8, filling K and L completely and putting all 8 remaining electrons in M (even though M could hold up to 18, the outermost-shell-of-8 rule caps it here). This pattern of numbers, written for each element, is called its electronic configuration.

where: outermost shell holds at most 8 electrons; inner shells fill before the next shell starts

sections.tip: When asked to write electron distribution for an element, first subtract 2 for K, then 8 for L, and put whatever remains (up to 8) in the next shell — show this subtraction as working, it is a marking step.

sections.heading: 4.4 Valency
sections.body:
The electrons present in the outermost shell of an atom are called valence electrons. It is these electrons that decide how an atom combines with other atoms, which is why the outermost shell is also called the valence shell.

Atoms with a completely filled outermost shell (8 electrons, or 2 for a K-shell-only atom like helium) show almost no chemical activity — these are the noble gases, and their combining capacity, or valency, is taken as zero.

For other atoms, valency is found from the number of valence electrons: (i) if the outermost shell has 1, 2, 3 or 4 electrons, the valency equals that number directly (the atom tends to lose these electrons); (ii) if the outermost shell has 5, 6 or 7 electrons, the valency is found by subtracting that number from 8 (the atom tends to gain electrons to complete its octet).

For example, sodium (2, 8, 1) has 1 valence electron, so its valency is 1. Magnesium (2, 8, 2) has valency 2. Chlorine (2, 8, 7) has 7 valence electrons, so its valency is 8 − 7 = 1. Oxygen (2, 6) has 6 valence electrons, so its valency is 8 − 6 = 2.

formulas.expr: if valence electrons ≤ 4, valency = number of valence electrons
if valence electrons > 4, valency = 8 − number of valence electrons

sections.tip: Always find the electronic configuration first, then read off the valence electrons from the last number — do not guess valency from memory for less familiar elements.

sections.heading: 4.5 Atomic Number and Mass Number
sections.body:
Every element has a fixed atomic number (Z), equal to the number of protons present in the nucleus of one atom of that element. Because an atom is neutral, the atomic number also equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom. Atomic number is the most fundamental identity of an element — it is what distinguishes one element from another.

The mass number (A) of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons present in its nucleus (its nucleons); electrons contribute negligible mass and are not counted. Protons and neutrons, being of almost equal mass and both present in the nucleus, together decide the mass of an atom.

An element is represented in full by writing its mass number as a left superscript and atomic number as a left subscript before its chemical symbol, for instance sodium is written as 2311Na, meaning 11 protons, 11 electrons and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons.

formulas.expr: atomic number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons (in a neutral atom)
mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons

sections.tip: In symbol questions like ᴬZX, always compute neutrons as A − Z before answering — a large fraction of marks are lost purely from arithmetic slips here.

sections.heading: 4.6 Isotopes and Isobars
sections.body:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, because they differ in the number of neutrons while having the same number of protons. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (11H, no neutron), deuterium (21H, 1 neutron) and tritium (31H, 2 neutrons). Carbon has isotopes carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14; chlorine occurs in nature mainly as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 in the ratio 3:1.

Because isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons and hence the same valence-electron arrangement, their chemical properties are identical; only their physical properties (like density) differ, since these depend on mass. This is why isotopes are placed at the same position in the periodic table.

Isotopes have important uses: an isotope of uranium (U-235) is used as fuel in nuclear reactors; an isotope of cobalt (Co-60) is used in the treatment of cancer; an isotope of iodine (I-131) is used in the treatment of goitre.

The average atomic mass of an element with isotopes is a weighted average of the isotopic masses, taken according to their relative natural abundance — for chlorine, (35 × 75 + 37 × 25)/100 = 35.5 u, which is why chlorine's atomic mass in the periodic table is not a whole number.

Isobars, by contrast, are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers, because their combined proton-plus-neutron counts happen to match even though the number of protons differs. A classic pair is calcium (atomic number 20) and argon (atomic number 18), both with mass number 40. Since isobars have different numbers of protons and electrons, they are different elements with different chemical properties.

formulas.expr: isotopes: same Z, different A (same element)
where: ¹H, ²H, ³H — same 1 proton, 0/1/2 neutrons

formulas.expr: isobars: same A, different Z (different elements)
average atomic mass = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance)/100

sections.tip: Do not mix up the two: same letters differ — isoTOPES share the same aTOmic number; isoBARS share the same mass numBer. Reading the words this way avoids the swap under exam pressure.

key_terms.definition: A fundamental, negatively charged sub-atomic particle (charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass ≈ 1/2000 u), discovered by J.J. Thomson using cathode rays.
A positively charged sub-atomic particle of mass about 1 u, discovered from canal (anode) rays by E. Goldstein; found in the nucleus.
An electrically neutral sub-atomic particle of mass about 1 u, discovered by J. Chadwick, present in the nucleus of all atoms except ordinary hydrogen.
The tiny, dense, positively charged core of an atom that contains almost all of its mass, made up of protons and neutrons.
Positively charged rays produced in a discharge tube containing a perforated cathode; they led to the discovery of the proton.
An atom is a uniformly positive sphere with electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding; the total positive and negative charges balance.
The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre with electrons revolving around it in orbits, and mostly empty space in between.
Electrons revolve only in certain fixed, discrete orbits (shells) without radiating energy, giving the atom a stable structure.
A fixed circular path, labelled K, L, M, N... (n = 1, 2, 3, 4...), in which electrons are permitted to revolve around the nucleus.
The electrons present in the outermost shell of an atom; they determine the atom's chemical behaviour and valency.
The combining capacity of an atom, decided by the number of electrons in its outermost shell, needed to gain, lose or share to complete 8 electrons.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; equal to the number of electrons in a neutral atom; unique to each element.
The total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) present in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, differing only in the number of neutrons.
Atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
The collective name for protons and neutrons, the particles that make up the nucleus and give the atom most of its mass.

diagrams.title: Thomson's plum-pudding model of the atom
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a large shaded circle (the sphere of positive charge) and scatter several small solid dots inside it labelled 'e⁻' (electrons), like seeds in a watermelon. Label the sphere 'positively charged matter, spread throughout the atom' and note underneath that total positive charge = total negative charge.

diagrams.title: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a source of alpha particles on the left sending parallel arrows towards a thin gold foil in the centre, with a circular fluorescent (zinc sulphide) screen surrounding the foil. Show most arrows passing straight through, a few bending at small angles near the foil, and one arrow bouncing almost straight back. Label the tiny region at the centre of the foil, where deflection originates, as the nucleus.

diagrams.title: Bohr's model of the atom (with shells)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a small central nucleus labelled with its positive charge, surrounded by 2-4 concentric circles labelled K, L, M, N moving outward. Place dots for electrons on each circle according to the 2n² rule for a chosen element (e.g. sodium: 2 on K, 8 on L, 1 on M), and mark the outermost electron(s) as the valence electrons.

diagrams.title: Electron distribution of sodium and chlorine (ionic bonding lead-in)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two separate nucleus-and-shell diagrams side by side: sodium with 2, 8, 1 and chlorine with 2, 8, 7. Circle the lone valence electron of sodium and the single vacancy in chlorine's outer shell, and add an arrow from sodium's electron to chlorine's shell to show the transfer that gives both atoms a stable octet.

ncert_questions.a: Canal rays are streams of positively charged particles produced in a discharge tube fitted with a perforated cathode. They travel in a direction opposite to the cathode rays, i.e. from the anode towards the cathode and out through the holes. Their discovery by E. Goldstein led to the discovery of the proton.

ncert_questions.q: If an atom contains one electron and one proton, will it carry any charge or not?
ncert_questions.a: No, the atom will not carry any charge. It will be electrically neutral because the negative charge of the one electron (−1 unit) is exactly balanced by the positive charge of the one proton (+1 unit). This atom is, in fact, a hydrogen atom.

ncert_questions.q: On the basis of Thomson's model of an atom, explain how the atom is neutral as a whole.
ncert_questions.a: According to Thomson's model, an atom consists of a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it, distributed in such a way that the magnitude of the positive charge on the sphere exactly equals the total negative charge carried by the embedded electrons. Since the total positive charge equals the total negative charge, the net charge on the atom is zero, so the atom is electrically neutral as a whole.

ncert_questions.q: On the basis of Rutherford's model of an atom, which sub-atomic particle is present in the nucleus of an atom?
ncert_questions.a: According to Rutherford's model, the nucleus of an atom contains the positively charged particles, i.e. protons; it is this concentrated positive charge in the nucleus that repelled the alpha particles in his scattering experiment. (After Chadwick's later discovery, we also know the nucleus contains neutrons, but Rutherford's own model, based on the scattering experiment, identified only the positive protons.)

ncert_questions.q: Draw a sketch of Bohr's model of an atom with three shells.
ncert_questions.a: The sketch should show a small central nucleus, and around it three concentric circles labelled K, L and M in order going outward, representing n = 1, 2, 3. Electrons are shown as dots placed on these circles, filled following the 2n² rule and the outer-shell-of-8 rule — for example for an atom with 13 electrons: 2 electrons on K, 8 on L and 3 on M (aluminium, 2, 8, 3).

ncert_questions.q: What do you think would be the observation if the alpha-particle scattering experiment is carried out using a foil of a metal other than gold?
ncert_questions.a: The general pattern of observations — most particles passing straight through, a few deflected, and a very small number bouncing back — would still be seen with any metal foil, because every atom has a small dense positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space. However, the exact amount of deflection would change with the metal's atomic number: a foil of a heavier metal (with a nucleus of greater positive charge and mass, such as lead) would cause more alpha particles to be deflected through larger angles than gold, while a much lighter metal (lower atomic number) would cause less deflection, because the repulsive/scattering force depends on the nuclear charge.

ncert_questions.q: Name the three sub-atomic particles of an atom.
ncert_questions.a: The three sub-atomic particles of an atom are the electron (negatively charged, discovered by J.J. Thomson), the proton (positively charged, discovered by E. Goldstein) and the neutron (no charge, discovered by J. Chadwick).

ncert_questions.q: Helium atom has an atomic mass of 4 u and two protons in its nucleus. How many neutrons does it have?
ncert_questions.a: Mass number (A) = 4, atomic number (Z) = number of protons = 2. Number of neutrons = A − Z = 4 − 2 = 2. So the helium atom has 2 neutrons.

ncert_questions.q: Write the distribution of electrons in carbon and sodium atoms.
ncert_questions.a: Carbon has atomic number 6, so it has 6 electrons: 2 in the K shell and the remaining 4 in the L shell — electron distribution 2, 4. Sodium has atomic number 11, so it has 11 electrons: 2 in K, 8 in L, and the remaining 1 in M — electron distribution 2, 8, 1.

ncert_questions.q: If K and L shells of an atom are full, then what would be the total number of electrons in the atom?
ncert_questions.a: The K shell (n = 1) holds a maximum of 2n² = 2 × 1² = 2 electrons, and the L shell (n = 2) holds a maximum of 2n² = 2 × 2² = 8 electrons. If both are completely full, the total number of electrons = 2 + 8 = 10 electrons. (This corresponds to the noble gas neon, atomic number 10.)

ncert_questions.q: How will you find the valency of chlorine, sulphur and magnesium?
ncert_questions.a:
Chlorine (atomic number 17): electron distribution 2, 8, 7. It has 7 valence electrons, which is more than 4, so valency = 8 − 7 = 1.

Sulphur (atomic number 16): electron distribution 2, 8, 6. It has 6 valence electrons, more than 4, so valency = 8 − 6 = 2.

Magnesium (atomic number 12): electron distribution 2, 8, 2. It has 2 valence electrons, which is 4 or less, so valency = 2 directly.

ncert_questions.q: If number of electrons in an atom is 8 and number of protons is also 8, then (i) what is the atomic number of the atom? and (ii) what is the charge on the atom?
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Atomic number = number of protons = 8.

(ii) Since the number of electrons (8, giving −8 units of charge) equals the number of protons (8, giving +8 units of charge), the positive and negative charges balance exactly, so the atom carries no net charge — it is electrically neutral (charge = 0). This is the oxygen atom.

ncert_questions.q: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment and state the conclusions drawn from it.
ncert_questions.a:
A stream of high-energy alpha particles from a radioactive source was directed at a thin gold foil (about 100 nm thick), surrounded by a circular fluorescent zinc sulphide screen that produced a flash of light wherever a particle struck it, letting Rutherford track how the particles scattered.

Observations: most alpha particles passed straight through the foil undeflected; a small fraction were deflected by small angles; a very small fraction (about 1 in 12000) rebounded almost back the way they came.

Conclusions: most of the atom's volume is empty space (since most particles passed through); a small region carries a concentrated positive charge that repels the positively charged alpha particles (giving the small-angle deflections); and this same tiny region contains almost all the atom's mass (since only a head-on collision with something massive could bounce a fast alpha particle straight back). This region was named the nucleus.

ncert_questions.q: For the symbols H, D and T, tabulate the three sub-atomic particles found in each of them.
ncert_questions.a:
H (protium, ¹₁H): 1 proton, 1 electron, 0 neutrons.

D (deuterium, ²₁H): 1 proton, 1 electron, 1 neutron.

T (tritium, ³₁H): 1 proton, 1 electron, 2 neutrons. All three have the same atomic number (1) but different mass numbers (1, 2, 3), so they are isotopes of hydrogen.

ncert_questions.q: Write the electronic configuration of any one pair of isotopes and one pair of isobars.
ncert_questions.a:
Isotopes — carbon-12 and carbon-14: both have atomic number 6, so both have the electronic configuration 2, 4; they differ only in the number of neutrons (6 and 8) inside the nucleus, which does not change the electron arrangement.

Isobars — calcium-40 (atomic number 20: 2, 8, 8, 2) and argon-40 (atomic number 18: 2, 8, 8): both have mass number 40 but different atomic numbers, so their electron distributions, and hence their chemical properties, are different.

pyq.q: Canal rays are streams of:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Canal rays, discovered by Goldstein, are positively charged particles moving from the anode towards the cathode; they led to the discovery of the proton.

pyq.q: Which scientist discovered the neutron?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: J. Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932; it is a neutral particle present in the nucleus of all atoms except ordinary hydrogen.

pyq.q: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, the very small number of alpha particles that bounced back almost 180° showed that:
options: The atom is mostly empty space
Almost the entire mass of the atom is concentrated in a very small region
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Only a head-on encounter with something both massive and small could send a fast alpha particle straight back, so this observation showed the mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

pyq.q: The maximum number of electrons that the M shell (n = 3) can hold is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Maximum electrons in a shell = 2n². For M, n = 3, so 2 × 3² = 18.

pyq.q: An atom with electron distribution 2, 8, 7 has a valency of:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Since the number of valence electrons (7) is more than 4, valency = 8 − 7 = 1. This is the configuration of chlorine.

pyq.q: Isotopes of an element have:
options: Same atomic number, different mass number
Same mass number, different atomic number
Different atomic number and different mass number
Same atomic number and same mass number
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons, giving different mass numbers.

pyq.q: An atom has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Its mass number is:
pyq.answer: b

pyq.q: Assertion (A): An atom is electrically neutral. Reason (R): The number of protons in an atom is always equal to the number of neutrons.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: An atom is neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons, not neutrons; protons and neutrons need not be equal (e.g. chlorine-37 has 17 protons and 20 neutrons). So A is true, R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Rutherford's model of the atom could not explain the stability of the atom. Reason (R): A revolving, accelerating charged particle is expected to continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: By classical electromagnetic theory, a revolving charge radiates energy; this would make the orbit shrink and the electron fall into the nucleus, so Rutherford's model failed to explain atomic stability — R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Isotopes of an element show identical chemical properties. Reason (R): Chemical properties are decided by the number of valence electrons, which is the same for all isotopes of an element.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number, so the same number of electrons and the same valence-electron arrangement, which decides chemical behaviour — hence identical chemical properties.

pyq.q: Name the scientist who discovered the electron and the experimental set-up used.
pyq.answer: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron using a cathode ray discharge tube experiment. Cathode rays, deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field, were shown to be streams of negatively charged particles present in the atoms of every element.

pyq.q: Give the electron distribution of an aluminium atom (atomic number 13) and state its valency.
pyq.answer: Aluminium (Z = 13): 2 electrons in K, 8 in L, and the remaining 3 in M — distribution 2, 8, 3. Since it has 3 valence electrons (≤ 4), its valency is 3.

pyq.q: What is the difference between isotopes and isobars? State one point only.
pyq.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different neutron count); isobars are atoms of different elements with different atomic numbers but the same mass number.

pyq.q: State the two postulates of Bohr's model of the atom.
pyq.answer: (i) Electrons revolve only in certain fixed, discrete orbits called shells or energy levels. (ii) While revolving in these fixed orbits, electrons do not radiate energy.

pyq.q: State three observations of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment.
pyq.answer: (i) Most of the fast-moving alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection. (ii) Some of the alpha particles were deflected through small angles. (iii) A very small fraction of alpha particles (about 1 in 12000) bounced back almost 180°.

pyq.q: An atom has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. Find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in it. Name the element.
pyq.answer: Number of protons = atomic number = 11. Number of electrons (neutral atom) = number of protons = 11. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12. Atomic number 11 corresponds to sodium (Na).

pyq.q: Give one difference each between an electron and a proton, and between a proton and a neutron.
pyq.answer: Electron vs proton: an electron carries a charge of −1 unit and a mass of about 1/2000 u, while a proton carries a charge of +1 unit and a mass of about 1 u — so they differ in both charge and mass. Proton vs neutron: a proton carries a charge of +1 unit while a neutron carries no charge, even though their masses are almost equal (about 1 u each).

pyq.q: Why does an atom of chlorine (2, 8, 7) have a valency of 1 while an atom of chlorine also forms compounds by gaining one electron — explain using the octet idea.
pyq.answer: Chlorine has 7 electrons in its outermost shell. To complete a stable octet (8 electrons), it needs just 1 more electron, so its combining capacity (valency) is 8 − 7 = 1. This single electron is usually gained from another atom (e.g. sodium), which is why chlorine typically forms compounds like NaCl by accepting one electron to complete its outer shell.

pyq.q: Describe Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment with a labelled diagram. State the observations and the conclusions drawn from each observation, and mention one drawback of the model he proposed.
pyq.answer:
Rutherford directed a beam of fast alpha particles from a radioactive source at a thin gold foil (about 100 nm thick) surrounded by a circular fluorescent zinc sulphide screen that flashed light where a particle struck it, letting the scattering pattern be recorded (diagram: source → narrow beam → gold foil at centre → circular ZnS screen around it, with most rays passing straight, a few bending, and one rebounding).

Observation 1: most alpha particles passed straight through without deflection. Conclusion: most of the space inside an atom is empty.

Observation 2: a small fraction were deflected through small angles. Conclusion: there is a concentration of positive charge inside the atom that repels the positively charged alpha particles.

Observation 3: a very small fraction (about 1 in 12000) bounced back almost 180°. Conclusion: this positive charge, and almost the entire mass of the atom, is concentrated in a very small region — the nucleus.

Drawback: Rutherford's model could not explain why electrons revolving around the nucleus do not lose energy and spiral into it, since an accelerating charge should radiate energy according to classical theory — so the model failed to account for the stability of the atom. This drawback was fixed later by Bohr, who proposed that electrons in fixed orbits do not radiate energy.

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of Bohr's model of the sodium atom and use it to explain the terms shell, valence electron and valency for sodium.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: a small central nucleus (containing 11 protons and 12 neutrons, net charge +11) with three concentric circles labelled K, L, M around it; 2 electron dots on K, 8 on L, and 1 on M.

Shell: a fixed circular path (K, L, M, ... for n = 1, 2, 3, ...) in which electrons are permitted to move around the nucleus, filled following the 2n² rule (K ≤ 2, L ≤ 8, M ≤ 8 as outermost here).

Valence electron: the electron(s) present in the outermost occupied shell — for sodium this is the single electron in the M shell.

Valency: since sodium has only 1 valence electron (4 or fewer), its valency equals that number directly, so sodium has a valency of 1; it readily loses this one electron to attain the stable configuration of neon (2, 8).

pyq.q: Explain, with examples, the difference between isotopes and isobars. Give the electron distribution for one example of each and state one industrial or medical use of an isotope.
pyq.answer:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, differing in the number of neutrons. Example: carbon-12 (6 protons, 6 neutrons) and carbon-14 (6 protons, 8 neutrons); both have electron distribution 2, 4 since both have atomic number 6. Isotopes have identical chemical properties because chemical behaviour depends on the number and arrangement of electrons, which is the same for all isotopes of an element; only physical properties like density differ.

Isobars are atoms of different elements with different atomic numbers but the same mass number. Example: calcium (atomic number 20, distribution 2, 8, 8, 2) and argon (atomic number 18, distribution 2, 8, 8), both with mass number 40. Because their number of protons and electrons differ, isobars are chemically different elements, unlike isotopes.

Use of an isotope: an isotope of cobalt, cobalt-60, is used in the radiation treatment of cancer.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
Chlorine, as found in nature, is actually a mixture of two kinds of atoms: about 75% of chlorine atoms have a mass number of 35, and about 25% have a mass number of 37. Both kinds have the same atomic number, 17, and the same chemical behaviour, which is why chlorine is listed in the periodic table as a single element with one average atomic mass.
(i) What name is given to atoms of the same element that have different mass numbers?
(ii) Find the number of neutrons in the chlorine atom of mass number 37.
(iii) Calculate the average atomic mass of chlorine using the abundances given.
(iv) Explain why both kinds of chlorine atoms show the same chemical properties even though their masses differ.
pyq.answer:
(i) They are called isotopes.

(ii) Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 37 − 17 = 20.

(iii) Average atomic mass = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25)/100 = (2625 + 925)/100 = 3550/100 = 35.5 u.

(iv) Both isotopes have the same atomic number (17), so both have the same number of electrons (17) and the same electron distribution (2, 8, 7). Since chemical properties are decided by the number and arrangement of electrons — especially the valence electrons — and not by the number of neutrons, both isotopes behave identically in chemical reactions.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
Before Rutherford's experiment, J.J. Thomson had proposed that an atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons studded inside it, much like seeds in a watermelon, with the total positive charge equal to the total negative charge. When Rutherford's students fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil to test this model, the results did not match what Thomson's model predicted, and a new model of the atom had to be proposed.
(i) What is Thomson's model of the atom commonly called?
(ii) Name one observation of the alpha-particle scattering experiment that Thomson's model could not explain, and say why.
(iii) What new sub-atomic feature did Rutherford propose to explain this observation?
(iv) State one drawback of the model Rutherford proposed in its place.
pyq.answer:
(i) It is commonly called the plum-pudding model (or watermelon model).

(ii) The observation that a very small fraction of alpha particles bounced back almost 180° could not be explained, because in Thomson's model the positive charge is spread thinly throughout the whole atom, so it could never repel a fast, massive alpha particle strongly enough to reverse its direction.

(iii) Rutherford proposed that the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, containing almost all the atom's mass, with electrons revolving around it and most of the atom being empty space.

(iv) Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom — a revolving, accelerating electron should, by classical theory, continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, which does not actually happen.

practice_mcq.explanation: Cathode rays bend towards the positive plate in an electric field, showing they are negatively charged; their study led Thomson to the electron.

practice_mcq.q: Which particle has a mass nearly equal to a proton but no electric charge?
practice_mcq.explanation: The neutron has a mass of about 1 u, close to the proton's mass, but carries no charge.

practice_mcq.q: In Thomson's model, the atom is compared to:
practice_mcq.explanation: Thomson pictured electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge, like seeds studded in a watermelon.

practice_mcq.q: According to Rutherford's model, most of the volume of an atom is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Since most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, most of the atom's volume must be empty space.

practice_mcq.q: Who proposed that electrons revolve in fixed, discrete orbits without radiating energy?
practice_mcq.explanation: This is one of Bohr's two postulates, proposed to fix the instability problem of Rutherford's model.

practice_mcq.q: The maximum number of electrons the L shell can hold is:
practice_mcq.explanation: For L, n = 2, so maximum electrons = 2n² = 2 × 4 = 8.

practice_mcq.q: An atom with electron distribution 2, 8, 2 has valency:
practice_mcq.explanation: 2 valence electrons (≤ 4), so valency = 2 directly. This is magnesium.

practice_mcq.q: An atom with electron distribution 2, 6 has valency:
practice_mcq.explanation: 6 valence electrons (> 4), so valency = 8 − 6 = 2. This is oxygen.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these correctly gives the number of neutrons in an atom?
practice_mcq.explanation: Neutrons = mass number (protons + neutrons) − atomic number (protons).

practice_mcq.q: Two atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called:
practice_mcq.explanation: Same atomic number, different mass number defines isotopes.

practice_mcq.q: Two atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called:
practice_mcq.explanation: Same mass number, different atomic number defines isobars, e.g. calcium-40 and argon-40.

practice_mcq.q: An isotope of which element is used as fuel in nuclear reactors?
practice_mcq.explanation: Uranium-235 is used as nuclear fuel; cobalt-60 is used in cancer treatment and iodine-131 in goitre treatment.

practice_mcq.q: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35 (this is chlorine-35).

practice_mcq.q: Noble gases have a valency of zero because:
options: Their outermost shell is completely filled
They have only one shell always
practice_mcq.explanation: A completely filled outermost shell (8 electrons, or 2 for helium) means no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so valency is zero.

practice_mcq.q: Deuterium and tritium are isotopes of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Protium, deuterium and tritium are the three isotopes of hydrogen, differing in neutron number (0, 1, 2).

practice_mcq.q: Which experiment provided the first evidence that an atom has a dense central nucleus?
practice_mcq.explanation: Rutherford's gold-foil alpha-particle scattering experiment revealed the existence of a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

common_mistakes: Mixing up isotopes and isobars — remember isoTOPES have the same aTOmic number, isoBARS have the same mass numBer.
Forgetting that valency for more than 4 valence electrons is found by subtracting from 8, not by using the valence electron count directly.
Writing the number of neutrons as mass number plus atomic number instead of mass number minus atomic number.
Believing that isotopes of an element have different chemical properties — they have identical chemical properties and differ only in mass-related physical properties.
Confusing which scientist discovered which particle: Thomson (electron, cathode rays), Goldstein (proton, canal rays), Chadwick (neutron).
Filling more than 8 electrons in an outermost shell just because 2n² allows it — the outermost-shell-of-8 rule overrides 2n² for the last shell.
Stating that Rutherford's model explained the stability of the atom — it is Bohr's model that fixed this drawback, not Rutherford's.
Skipping the 'inner shell must be filled first' rule and jumping electrons into an outer shell before the inner one is complete.
strategy:
This chapter rewards a clear timeline more than rote memorisation: know what each scientist discovered, with which apparatus, and exactly what drawback led to the next model — Thomson (plum-pudding, cathode rays) → Rutherford (nucleus, alpha-scattering, but unstable) → Bohr (fixed orbits, stable). Practise drawing all three model diagrams and the alpha-scattering set-up until you can label them from memory; a labelled diagram is worth marks on its own in the 5-mark question.

Drill the 2n² rule and the outermost-shell-of-8 rule with electron distributions for the first twenty elements (H to Ca) until you can write them without hesitation — every valency, atomic number/mass number, and isotope/isobar question builds on this. Memorise the definitions of atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars word for word as NCERT states them, since examiners check for precise language.

Keep a short table of the standard examples: hydrogen's three isotopes, carbon-12/13/14, chlorine-35/37, and the calcium-argon isobar pair — these come back repeatedly in VSA, SA and case-based questions. Finish by working the average-atomic-mass calculation for chlorine at least twice by hand so the arithmetic is automatic.
revision_checklist: Can state charge and mass of electron, proton and neutron, and who discovered each
Can describe Thomson's plum-pudding model and explain why the atom is neutral in it
Can describe the alpha-particle scattering experiment set-up, its three observations and three conclusions
Can state the one major drawback of Rutherford's model and how Bohr's postulates fixed it
Can state both of Bohr's postulates in exact words
Can apply the 2n² rule and the outermost-8 rule to write electron distribution for any element up to Z = 20
Can find valency from electron distribution for both ≤ 4 and > 4 valence-electron cases
Can define atomic number and mass number and compute neutrons as A − Z
Can write the full ᴬZX symbol for a given element with proton/neutron/electron count
Can distinguish isotopes from isobars and give one worked example of each
Can list at least two practical uses of isotopes (uranium-235, cobalt-60, iodine-131)
Can calculate an element's average atomic mass from isotopic abundances (e.g. chlorine)
Can draw and label all three atomic model diagrams and the gold-foil experiment diagram
